ingestion.notes: Figures and supplementary tables were not available in the text; results are described from the main text.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: GPT-4, given a cluster's top marker or differential genes, names the cell type in close agreement with expert labels, and beats SingleR, ScType and CellMarker 2.0 on ten datasets.

sections.heading: Question
sections.body: Can a general-purpose large language model replace the manual step of matching each cluster's highly expressed genes to known marker genes?

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: The authors built GPTCelltype, an R package that turns per-cluster gene lists into a prompt ('Identify cell types of <tissue> cells using the following markers…') and sends it to GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 through the OpenAI API. They tested basic, chain-of-thought and repeated (majority-of-five) prompts, and top 10/20/30 genes from Wilcoxon or t-tests.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.body: Ten datasets across five species and hundreds of tissue and cell types, including normal tissue (HuBMAP Azimuth, GTEx, Human and Mouse Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens) and cancer (B-cell lymphoma, lung and colon cancer). Each prediction was mapped to Cell Ontology terms and scored 1 (full match), 0.5 (partial, same broad type) or 0 (mismatch) against the original authors' manual labels. Simulations tested mixed cell types, unknown cell types, missing genes and noisy gene lists.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: GPT-4 fully or partially matched manual labels for over 75% of cell types in most studies and tissues, and did best with literature-derived markers and with the top ten Wilcoxon genes; prompt strategy made little difference. It was strongest on immune cells and weaker on subtypes, very small clusters (≤10 cells) and B-lymphoma malignant cells. It separated pure from mixed types with 93% accuracy and known from unknown with 99%, and gave the same answer 85% of the time on repeated queries. API cost stayed under $0.10 for all queries in the study.

key_findings: Top 10 differential genes from a two-sided Wilcoxon test is the best input
Outperformed SingleR, ScType and CellMarker 2.0 on average agreement score
Some 'mismatches' were GPT-4 being more specific than the manual label (e.g. fibroblast vs. stromal cell)
Major types are matched more often than fine subtypes such as CD4 memory T cells
limitations: Training data are undisclosed, so the basis for an annotation can't be checked; the authors recommend expert validation
Risk of hallucination; noisy or unreliable differential genes degrade results
Datasets published before GPT-4's September 2021 training cutoff may have been seen in training
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred). This is the baseline the project's agent has to beat: an LLM annotating clusters from marker lists, with a reusable scoring scheme (Cell Ontology full/partial/mismatch) we can adopt for our own benchmarks.

sequencing.summary: Reuses published datasets; no new sequencing.

quantification.summary: Count matrices taken from the original studies.

preprocessing.summary: Library-size normalization and log1p transform of raw counts; differential genes per cell type with Seurat FindAllMarkers (Wilcoxon or t-test, logFC ≥ 0.25, detected in ≥10% of cells).

dimensionality_reduction.summary: Not part of the method; it starts from cluster-level gene lists.

batch_correction.summary: Some source datasets were batch-corrected by their original authors (e.g. ComBat for GTEx); not performed here.

clustering.summary: Uses the original authors' clusters / manual cell type groups as given.

annotation.summary: GPT-4 is prompted with each cluster's top differential or marker genes and the tissue name, and returns one cell type per cluster; results are scored against manual labels via Cell Ontology terms.
methods: LLM prompting with marker gene lists
